input: The Chilton-Colburn analogy is a very handy result at this point, because it allows us to connect the mass-transfer behaviour we are interested in with the friction behaviour that we already know about. What the Chilton-Colburn analogy says, in essence, is that $j_D$ is equal to half of the friction factor $f$, and we can quickly check the arithmetic of this on some values that are already in hand. At a Reynolds number of 20000, for instance, a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 leads straight to $j_D$ = 0.0032, which is just half the friction factor. It is important to remember, however, that this equality only really holds where the boundary layer treats momentum transfer and mass transfer in the same sort of way. If form drag is contributing to $f$, then the friction factor contains an element that has no counterpart on the mass-transfer side, and $j_D$ will fall below $f$ / 2; and if the transfer rate is high enough to start changing the boundary layer itself, the equality will break down once again. So a check of this kind does no more than confirm the arithmetic on that single pair of values, and it certainly does not extend the analogy into any new territory.
target: The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor $f$, and the equality is the form in which the analogy does its work. On values already in hand the arithmetic is direct: at a Reynolds number of 20000, a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 gives $j_D$ = 0.0032. The equality holds only where the boundary layer treats momentum and mass alike. Where form drag contributes to $f$, the friction factor carries a part with no mass-transfer counterpart and $j_D$ falls below $f$ / 2; where the transfer rate is high enough to change the boundary layer, the equality fails again, for the same reason in another dress: the measured friction no longer describes the layer across which the mass is moving. A check of this kind verifies the arithmetic on one pair of values. It extends the analogy to no new case, and a case with form drag or a high transfer rate takes its mass-transfer factor from measurement, or from a correlation built for that case, rather than from the friction factor it happens to have. The analogy is used inside its range or not at all, and the statement of the range is part of the result the excerpt leaves on the page.
